title: How do you decide what platform your agent will build your game in?
author: Camenwolf
selftext:
I find this very confusing.  To be clear, I've only build one game using Codex.  I love it.  The whole process has gone very well, but before I ever gave it the first prompt I decided what platform to build it in (Phaser 3.90.0). 

I'd like to start a new one.

I see all sort of videos on YouTube where people are like "look at this game I made with one prompt" or look what I did with Claude Code or Codex or whatever, but they never say what it is built in.  Did they tell the model what framework or platform to use?

I'm guessing for the 3D games (which is most of them) it's three.js, but they never EVER say that.  If I don't specify the platform, does the agent just pick one?

comments.author: ItsAlwaysTerminal
comments.body: I would argue that for any serious development and future extensibility you would want to build in an established engine like Unity, Godot, or UE. My preference being Godot because it's open source using an MCP even though they take a slightly harder line officially against AI.

replies.body: Eh, [https://github.com/yanhuifair/Godot-MCP](https://github.com/yanhuifair/Godot-MCP) and [https://github.com/hi-godot/godot-ai](https://github.com/hi-godot/godot-ai) have worked well for me depending on what part of development I am working in. replies.body:

replies.body: These MCP tools have built in tools for that, yanhuifair's MCP even does deterministic frame stepping to recreate more complex issues.

replies.author: Historical-D-Dog
replies.body: Você sente uma diferença muito grande usando isso, comparado a usar apenas a engine?

replies.author: ItsAlwaysTerminal
replies.body:
If I understood the question as "Do you notice a significant difference versus just using the AI agent?" the answer is yes, a massive difference. 

There many reasons for this including future modular design and how I improve larger projects over time. If someone is just making a Flappy Bird clone it doesnt matter, just throw it in three.js and call it a day. Any serious game development work should be build on a more robust framework imo. It makes it much easier if it becomes successful for future development, to manage the codebase as it gets larger, managing assets or changing design structures later. If you start by just having a model one shot some proprietary massive javascript game its gonna be a nightmare to manage if it becomes a bigger project even from the standpoint of token utilization as it has to ingest huge amounts of the project to understand the repo. All the engines I listed at their outset are structured in a way that a properly prompted/oriented harness will know how to navigate the project structure without having to read over tons of useless context that also worsens the outputs of your later prompts. Design principles do still matter.

replies.author: Historical-D-Dog
replies.body:
Thank you for the answers, that's what I wanted to know.
I don't know the overall quality of Reddit's translation, but that's what I was asking.

replies.author: Camenwolf
replies.body: Yeah.  I've never used Godot, but I've seen a lot of tutorials on it.  But my question really is more about, do most people start by giving the engine a prompt with a design goal in mind and letting it chose a framework, or do they decide what they want to build their game in and incorporate that into the prompt?  It's frustrating because I've watched a thousand videos of games people have built using agents.  They \*always\* say what agent they used.  They \*never\* say what engine it used to build the game.

replies.author: ItsAlwaysTerminal
replies.body: I always specify because I always build in Godot for a list of reasons. I develop an entire PRD and then hand Claude Code or Codex the PRD and work through it in stages. Roadmapping, implementation plans, etc

replies.author: affabledrunk
replies.body: Its like anything with AI. You ask the AI whats best. In my case after discussing we concluded that raw node front end with a c++ back-end deamon was the best way to do it, but that really cme out of a dicussion of what th goals were, what type of game, how to test it and distribniut etc.

comments.author: Kindly_Release5869
comments.body: I’m using Odin. How did I decide - well I know and like Odin so I’ll be able to code alongside as well.

comments.author: Snoo-29395
comments.body:
Avoid any "look what i did in 1 prompt". If you want to do something serious, it will take time and months of going back and forward.

The difference is that now you can maybe spent 4 months in something that would've taken 2 years before AI, but nothing good can come from a one-prompt game.

That being said, the engine depends on what you want to do.

I personally prefer Unreal Engine, but i'm making a 3D game, it would be a different story if i was planning on doing a visual novel or a 2D for example.

replies.author: Snoo-29395
replies.body: And i don't think three.js is the best approach, people uses it because the modeling is based on coding, something the AI works better with, but i've never in my life hear of a successful game using a JS library as the game engine.

comments.author: Coindk
comments.body: I asked specifically for Godot because I also want to learn how to work with it. There's nothing better than using AI to create some project from A to Z and modify or correct what it's doing by hand.
